title: Plant Ecology & Field Course I
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 300L Plant Ecology & Field Course I curriculum: vegetation sampling methods, quantitative community parameters, diversity indices, succession (seres), Nigerian vegetation zones, plant life-form classification, and phytosociology.

questions.question: In quantitative vegetation analysis, 'frequency' of a species refers to:
options: The percentage of sampling units (e.g., quadrats) in which the species occurs
The total number of individuals of the species counted
The percentage ground area covered by the species
The height of the tallest individual of the species
questions.correct_answer: The percentage of sampling units (e.g., quadrats) in which the species occurs
questions.explanation: Frequency measures how often (in what proportion of sample plots) a species is present, indicating its distributional pattern rather than its abundance.

questions.question: 'Density' of a plant species in a community is defined as:
options: The number of individuals of that species per unit area
The percentage of quadrats containing the species
The percentage of ground surface covered by that species
The total biomass of the species
questions.correct_answer: The number of individuals of that species per unit area
questions.explanation: Density expresses the abundance of a species as a count of individuals relative to a standard unit of area, distinguishing it from frequency and cover.

questions.question: 'Cover' in phytosociological studies refers to:
options: The percentage of ground area occupied by the vertical projection of a species' aerial parts
The number of quadrats sampled
The total number of species in the community
The distance between individual plants
questions.correct_answer: The percentage of ground area occupied by the vertical projection of a species' aerial parts
questions.explanation: Cover estimates the proportion of ground shaded or occupied when a species' canopy is projected vertically downward, useful for species like grasses where counting individuals is impractical.

questions.question: The Importance Value Index (IVI) of a species in a plant community is typically calculated by summing its:
options: Relative density, relative frequency, and relative dominance (or basal area)
Height, girth, and leaf area only
Relative frequency and species richness only
Total rainfall and temperature tolerance
questions.correct_answer: Relative density, relative frequency, and relative dominance (or basal area)
questions.explanation: IVI combines three relative values (density, frequency, and dominance/basal area, each as a percentage of the community total) to give an overall measure of a species' ecological importance, commonly out of 300.

questions.question: A quadrat is generally considered an appropriate minimum sampling size for a vegetation study when:
options: Increasing quadrat size no longer results in a significant increase in the number of species recorded (the species-area curve plateaus)
It is exactly one square metre regardless of vegetation type
It contains at least 100 individual plants
It matches the size of the entire study site
questions.correct_answer: Increasing quadrat size no longer results in a significant increase in the number of species recorded (the species-area curve plateaus)
questions.explanation: The minimal (or minimum representative) quadrat size is determined using a species-area curve; the point where the curve flattens indicates an adequately sized sampling unit.

questions.question: The Shannon-Wiener diversity index is a measure that combines:
options: Species richness and the evenness of individuals distributed among those species
Only the total number of species present
Only the total number of individuals present
Only the size of the sampled area
questions.correct_answer: Species richness and the evenness of individuals distributed among those species
questions.explanation: The Shannon-Wiener index (H') accounts for both how many species are present and how evenly individuals are distributed across them; a community with more species and more even abundance has a higher H'.

questions.question: Simpson's Diversity Index is based on the probability that:
options: Two individuals randomly selected from a community belong to different species
A species will go locally extinct
All species have equal frequency
The community has reached climax
questions.correct_answer: Two individuals randomly selected from a community belong to different species
questions.explanation: Simpson's index estimates the probability that two randomly drawn individuals are of different species; higher values (closer to 1) indicate greater diversity.

questions.question: The vertical layering of vegetation in a community, such as canopy, understorey, shrub, and ground layers in a forest, is referred to as:
options: Stratification
Zonation
Succession
Dominance
questions.correct_answer: Stratification
questions.explanation: Stratification describes the vertical structural organisation of a plant community into distinct layers, which is especially pronounced in tropical rainforests.

questions.question: Raunkiaer's life-form classification system categorises plants mainly according to:
options: The position of their perennating (surviving) buds relative to the soil surface during unfavourable seasons
Their flower colour
Their mode of pollination
Their fruit type
questions.correct_answer: The position of their perennating (surviving) buds relative to the soil surface during unfavourable seasons
questions.explanation: Raunkiaer classified plants (phanerophytes, chamaephytes, hemicryptophytes, cryptophytes, therophytes) based on how well-protected their surviving buds are, reflecting adaptation to climate.

questions.question: In Raunkiaer's system, 'phanerophytes' are plants whose perennating buds are:
options: Borne well above the ground on aerial shoots, as in trees and shrubs
Located at or just below the soil surface
Buried deep in the soil as bulbs or rhizomes
Present only as dormant seeds
questions.correct_answer: Borne well above the ground on aerial shoots, as in trees and shrubs
questions.explanation: Phanerophytes carry their renewal buds exposed on tall aerial shoots, typical of trees and large shrubs found abundantly in favourable, less harsh climates like the tropics.

questions.question: Ecological succession that begins in a newly formed body of water (such as a pond) and progresses toward a terrestrial climax is called a:
options: Hydrosere
Xerosere
Lithosere
Psammosere
questions.correct_answer: Hydrosere
questions.explanation: A hydrosere is the successional sequence starting in open water, passing through submerged, floating, and emergent vegetation stages, and eventually leading to marsh, then terrestrial vegetation.

questions.question: A successional sequence that begins on bare rock is called a:
options: Lithosere
Hydrosere
Halosere
Psammosere
questions.correct_answer: Lithosere
questions.explanation: A lithosere begins with pioneer organisms such as lichens colonising bare rock, gradually forming soil that supports mosses, herbs, and eventually woody vegetation.

questions.question: A successional sequence that begins on loose, shifting sand, such as coastal or riverine dunes, is called a:
options: Psammosere
Lithosere
Hydrosere
Hydrarch succession
questions.correct_answer: Psammosere
questions.explanation: A psammosere develops on sandy substrates, typically starting with sand-binding pioneer grasses that stabilise dunes before further succession can proceed.

questions.question: The monoclimax theory of succession, proposed by Clements, holds that:
options: All communities in a given climatic region will eventually converge on a single, climate-determined climax type
Multiple different stable climax communities can exist within the same climatic region
Succession never reaches a stable endpoint
Climax vegetation is determined solely by soil type
questions.correct_answer: All communities in a given climatic region will eventually converge on a single, climate-determined climax type
questions.explanation: Clements' monoclimax theory proposes that, given enough time, all seres within a climatic region converge toward one climatically-determined climax, regardless of the starting substrate.

questions.question: The polyclimax theory, in contrast to the monoclimax theory, proposes that:
options: A region may support several distinct stable climax communities, controlled by local factors such as soil, topography, and drainage, not climate alone
Only one type of climax vegetation can exist per continent
Succession always proceeds in exactly the same sequence everywhere
Climax communities cannot be influenced by soil conditions
questions.correct_answer: A region may support several distinct stable climax communities, controlled by local factors such as soil, topography, and drainage, not climate alone
questions.explanation: The polyclimax theory (Tansley) recognises that edaphic, topographic, and other local factors, not climate alone, can produce multiple stable climax types within one climatic region.

questions.question: Nigeria's vegetation zones, from south to north, generally follow the sequence:
options: Mangrove/coastal swamp, tropical rainforest, derived savanna, Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna, Sahel savanna
Sahel savanna, Sudan savanna, rainforest, mangrove
Desert, rainforest, savanna, mangrove
Guinea savanna, mangrove, rainforest, Sahel
questions.correct_answer: Mangrove/coastal swamp, tropical rainforest, derived savanna, Guinea savanna, Sudan savanna, Sahel savanna
questions.explanation: Nigeria's vegetation transitions with decreasing rainfall from the humid coast northward: coastal/mangrove swamp forest, rainforest, derived (transitional) savanna, then Guinea, Sudan, and Sahel savannas.

questions.question: The 'derived savanna' zone of Nigeria is understood to have originated mainly through:
options: Human clearance and repeated burning of what was formerly rainforest
Natural climatic desertification only
Volcanic activity destroying forest cover
Marine flooding of coastal forest
questions.correct_answer: Human clearance and repeated burning of what was formerly rainforest
questions.explanation: Derived savanna is a secondary, anthropogenic vegetation type resulting from long-term forest clearance, farming, and burning in the transition zone between the rainforest and Guinea savanna belts.

questions.question: Mangrove vegetation, found along Nigeria's coastline, is specially adapted to its saline, waterlogged habitat mainly through:
options: Specialised aerial roots (pneumatophores or stilt/prop roots) for gas exchange, and salt-tolerance mechanisms
Deep taproots reaching fresh groundwater far below the surface
Complete absence of a root system
Extremely reduced leaf surface with no stomata
questions.correct_answer: Specialised aerial roots (pneumatophores or stilt/prop roots) for gas exchange, and salt-tolerance mechanisms
questions.explanation: Mangroves such as Rhizophora (prop roots) and Avicennia (pneumatophores) have evolved aerial root adaptations to obtain oxygen in waterlogged, anoxic mud, along with physiological salt tolerance/exclusion.

questions.question: The Guinea savanna, one of Nigeria's major vegetation belts, is typically characterised by:
options: A mix of grassland with scattered, often fire-tolerant trees, and a marked wet and dry season
Continuous closed-canopy evergreen forest with no dry season
Permanently submerged aquatic vegetation
Complete absence of woody plants
questions.correct_answer: A mix of grassland with scattered, often fire-tolerant trees, and a marked wet and dry season
questions.explanation: Guinea savanna vegetation consists of a grass layer interspersed with scattered, often deciduous and fire-resistant trees, shaped by a pronounced seasonal rainfall pattern and regular bush fires.

questions.question: In field vegetation studies, the belt transect method differs from a simple line transect in that a belt transect:
options: Records vegetation within a defined strip (width) along the transect line, not just what intersects the line itself
Uses only a single point along the entire study area
Cannot be used to study zonation
Requires no measuring tape
questions.correct_answer: Records vegetation within a defined strip (width) along the transect line, not just what intersects the line itself
questions.explanation: A belt transect samples all vegetation within a measured width along the line, providing more detailed quantitative data (density, cover) than a simple line transect, which only records intersections.

questions.question: The point-quadrat (or point-intercept) method of vegetation sampling records vegetation by:
options: Lowering thin pins vertically at fixed points and noting which species each pin touches
Counting all species visible from a fixed distance
Weighing all plant biomass in a plot
Measuring only the tallest plant at each sample point
questions.correct_answer: Lowering thin pins vertically at fixed points and noting which species each pin touches
questions.explanation: In the point-quadrat method, a frame with vertical pins is lowered at sample points; each species touched by a pin is recorded, giving an unbiased estimate of cover, especially in grassland vegetation.

questions.question: 'Ecological amplitude' of a species refers to:
options: The range of environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, moisture, pH) under which the species can survive and reproduce
The physical size range of individuals within the species
The number of individuals of the species in one quadrat
The geographic distance between two populations
questions.correct_answer: The range of environmental conditions (e.g., temperature, moisture, pH) under which the species can survive and reproduce
questions.explanation: Ecological amplitude describes the breadth of environmental tolerance of a species; species with wide amplitude are generalists, while those with narrow amplitude are specialists confined to specific conditions.

questions.question: Dominance in a plant community, as used in phytosociology, is best measured by which parameter for tree species?
options: Basal area (cross-sectional area of stems at breast height)
Number of leaves per tree
Distance between individual trees
Height of the shortest tree only
questions.correct_answer: Basal area (cross-sectional area of stems at breast height)
questions.explanation: Dominance for woody species is typically estimated from basal area (derived from girth or diameter at breast height), reflecting the relative space and resources a species occupies in the canopy.

questions.question: Microclimate, as studied in plant ecology field courses, refers to:
options: The localised climatic conditions in and immediately around a specific small habitat, which may differ from the general regional climate
Only the average rainfall of an entire country
The internal temperature of individual plant cells
Global climate patterns over centuries
questions.correct_answer: The localised climatic conditions in and immediately around a specific small habitat, which may differ from the general regional climate
questions.explanation: Microclimate describes fine-scale variation in temperature, humidity, light, and wind within a small area (e.g., forest floor versus canopy), often markedly different from the broader regional macroclimate.

questions.question: In field sampling, an 'indicator species' is one that:
options: Is closely associated with particular environmental conditions and whose presence signals those conditions
Occurs in every habitat regardless of conditions
Is always the most abundant species present
Cannot be identified without DNA analysis
questions.correct_answer: Is closely associated with particular environmental conditions and whose presence signals those conditions
questions.explanation: Indicator species have narrow ecological tolerances tied to specific conditions (e.g., soil acidity or waterlogging), so their presence or absence can indicate the state of the environment.

questions.question: A 'synusia' in plant community ecology refers to:
options: A group of plant species with a similar life form or growth habit occupying the same layer of a community
The total number of plants in a quadrat
A single individual plant
The soil profile beneath a community
questions.correct_answer: A group of plant species with a similar life form or growth habit occupying the same layer of a community
questions.explanation: A synusia is a structural/functional subunit of a plant community comprising species with similar growth form (e.g., the epiphyte synusia or the herb layer synusia) occupying a shared microhabitat or stratum.

questions.question: Random sampling in vegetation studies is preferred over subjective (selective) placement of quadrats mainly because random sampling:
options: Reduces observer bias and allows valid statistical analysis of the data
Always requires fewer quadrats
Guarantees every species will be recorded
Eliminates the need for replicate sampling
questions.correct_answer: Reduces observer bias and allows valid statistical analysis of the data
questions.explanation: Random placement of sampling units avoids the observer unconsciously favouring particular patches, and it satisfies the assumptions underlying most standard statistical tests applied to the data.

questions.question: The 'relative frequency' of a species in a community is calculated as:
options: (Frequency of the species / sum of frequencies of all species) multiplied by 100
Total number of individuals of the species only
Frequency of the species divided by total number of quadrats sampled without multiplying by 100
Number of species present in the community
questions.correct_answer: (Frequency of the species / sum of frequencies of all species) multiplied by 100
questions.explanation: Relative frequency expresses a species' frequency value as a percentage of the total frequency values summed across all species in the community, used in calculating the Importance Value Index.

questions.question: A field ecology practical that involves recording temperature, light intensity, humidity, and soil pH alongside vegetation data is primarily aimed at:
options: Correlating abiotic (environmental) factors with the observed pattern of species distribution and abundance
Determining the exact age of each plant sampled
Classifying plants taxonomically into families
Measuring the rate of photosynthesis in real time
questions.correct_answer: Correlating abiotic (environmental) factors with the observed pattern of species distribution and abundance
questions.explanation: Recording abiotic parameters alongside vegetation data allows ecologists to relate environmental gradients to observed patterns of plant zonation, dominance, and community composition.
